source.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration

page_placements.theme: Decodability is not control: the best-separating layer or direction is not the causal refusal handle

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: The study tests difference-in-means abliteration and evaluates a defense trained to make harmful and benign activations inseparable along that estimate. It finds that the edit has little effect on INSEP-trained models, and also evaluates a multi-directional removal attack.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own measurements of activation separability and outcomes of weight-edit attacks. Rows cover those results, including the standard difference-in-means attack and the comparison with SOM. Results cited from other studies are not rows. The broader leaderboard's results for other attack types are omitted because they do not test these claim versions. The paper does not measure activation addition or general capability after abliteration; capability scores are for defended models before attack.
record.test_reason: The study applies difference-in-means weight ablation (and Heretic, SOM, ACE) to eight undefended instruction-tuned models, with harm scores. It then shows refusal surviving that ablation once a fine-tuned defense (INSEP) collapses the direction's separability. These results bear on V1, V2, V7, and more weakly on V4. Reimplemented ReFAT/ART results bear on V3's robustness clause.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add three points. The authors report that INSEP drives diff-in-means separability to chance while classes stay separable along an LDA direction. They report that the separability term mainly resists Heretic and ACE, not plain ablation, which behavioural terms already cover (Table 7). They call multi-direction SOM the main remaining weakness and leave collapsing higher-order axes untested.
record.recipe_differences: INSEP trains an adapter to reduce harmful–benign separability along a recomputed difference-in-means direction while behavior losses preserve base responses. The evaluation applies published weight-edit attacks, including all-layer difference-in-means ablation; it is not a reproduction of the original study's full causal intervention suite.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by defense and base model. INSEP's null-referenced layer-selection variant is reported as competitive on Qwen2.5-7B but substantially worse than unfiltered INSEP on Mistral-7B-v0.3 (Appendix H). Disjoint attack-corpus estimation leaves INSEP's measured attack harm low.

fits_no_version.finding: A whitened (LDA) direction separates classes near-perfectly (AUC 1.000/.999). Ablating it partially raises harm on the base model (.08→.395) but fails on INSEP (.036). The authors argue it tracks prompt content, not refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear separability of harmful/benign activations along a direction does not imply that direction mediates refusal.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code may be made available to reviewers during rebuttal, but it is not included at submission
record.problems: The core separability and matched rank-1 attack analyses are on Llama-3.2-1B; the standard leaderboard reports harmfulness scores rather than refusal rates. The paper does not report general-capability measurements after the ablation edit. The disjoint-corpus comparison is reported in text without uncertainty. Some headline attack results aggregate across seeds, and the text notes that its attack suite is not exhaustive and does not include position-searching attacks.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the leaderboard's ACE, Heretic, SOM (except the aggregate INSEP comparison), prefill, utility, and MMLU values where they do not directly test the recorded versions; also omitted other defense methods' ablation results. These appear in Tables 2 and 20–26. Omitted cited results from prior papers and the training-pool, objective-term, and hyperparameter-search results.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; capability retention after ablation. Utility and MMLU are measured on defended models before attack, and a JSD penalty constrains attack layer choice.
Capability of abliterated models; community-released abliterated checkpoints.
Whether prompt jailbreaks work by suppressing the direction.
Direct geometric characterisation (affine, cone, subspace). Only attack-strength comparisons are reported.
All. Qwen3-14B is included but not analysed as a reasoning model.

missing.what: Heretic (optimised diff-in-means abliteration) harm on undefended base models: .832, .806, .847, .893, .847, .563, .840, .928. Also INSEP Heretic harm (mean .081).
missing.locator: Tables 2, 11, 20–26, Heretic column, base and INSEP rows

missing.what: Unablated harm on undefended Llama-3.2-1B ≈0.08 (baseline for abl rows).
Mean harm by attack on undefended base models: SOM .418 vs abl .455, ACE .462.
ReFAT and ART abl/prefill harm vs undefended (ReFAT abl .643, prefill .503; ART abl .368, prefill .286; base .455/.339).
Objective ablation: dropping the separability term leaves abl harm at .054 (vs .084 full). The behavioural refusal terms alone resist diff-in-means ablation.

record.verdict_notes: Harm is StrongREJECT on CatQA, not refusal rate, so intermediate scores on small models are hard to read as incomplete refusal removal. INSEP is a deliberately trained defense, so its results speak to V7 and to V1/V2 scope, not to naturally arising structure. ReFAT/ART are reimplementations without public code, which weakens the V3 verdicts. Code is not released, and the paper is under review.

versions.untested_parts: Tests difference-in-means removal, activation separability, and harmful-response outcomes for selected attacks. Does not test adding the direction to induce refusal, nor whether other abilities remain intact after ablating it.
Evaluates weight-edit attacks on instruction-tuned base models and INSEP-trained models. Does not evaluate all released models or establish post-ablation retention of general capability.
Does not test whether prompt jailbreaks suppress this direction or whether training specifically against its ablation improves jailbreak robustness.
Compares difference-in-means removal with a multi-direction SOM attack. Does not directly establish whether refusal is geometrically affine, conical, or a dominant direction plus others.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test of the direction.
INSEP is trained to reduce separability while preserving behavior, but the study does not test when or how refusal training determines whether one removable direction exists.

relation.reason: Its own results measure how far DIM weight ablation raises harm on undefended and trained models.

tranche.reason: The study is mainly a defense paper. It also reports DIM ablation on eight undefended bases, with incomplete or weak removal on five of them. It shows refusal surviving DIM ablation after INSEP training and argues refusal is carried beyond the linear DIM direction. These results bear on V1, V2 and V7.

source_check.notes: The pack gives no [lN] ids, so l1–l12 follow the order the verdicts are listed in. The ICLR page footer is addressed to human reviewers and is not an instruction to an AI. Unattacked harm is stated only for undefended Llama-3.2-1B (0.08). Attack directions come from the final prompt token only (300 prompts per class). ReFAT, ART and AMRA are reimplemented without public code. Per-base results for ReFAT, ART and SOM are mixed, and the Table 11 means hide this.

statements.correction: INSEP leaderboard DIM-ablation harm: Llama-3.2-1B .084, OLMo-2-1B .097, Gemma-2-2B .033, Qwen2.5-7B .052, OLMo-2-13B .020, Phi-4 .006, Qwen3-14B .033 (Tables 2, 20–26). Mistral-7B-v0.3: INSEP .318 vs .720 undefended (Table 23). Llama-3.2-1B matched rank-1 attack: .032±.008 (Table 10). INSEP trains a LoRA adapter to reduce DIM separability, with refusal/compliance/prefill losses; it applies no ablation during training.
statements.problem: Three errors. Llama-3.2-1B .032 comes from the separate matched-attack analysis (Table 10), not the leaderboard behind the .006–.097 range. The defended range is set against undefended Mistral without giving INSEP Mistral's .318. Cited row r25 is undefended Phi-4 (.097); the .006 is r26. Also, the conditions list INSEP among defenses that train against ablation, which it does not.

statements.correction: Qwen3-14B undefended: DIM ablation harm .647, Heretic .928. INSEP-defended: abl .033 (Table 26). The layer is chosen by a min-refusal sweep with a JSD penalty, and the projection is applied at all layers (Table 34).
statements.problem: .033 is only the INSEP-defended model. On undefended Qwen3-14B the same study finds ablation works, which puts it on the 'against' side.

statements.correction: Gemma-2-2B undefended: abl .121, Heretic .847 (Table 22). The direction is estimated at the final prompt token from 300 contrast prompts per class. The layer is picked by a min-refusal sweep with a JSD penalty, and the projection (alpha=1.0) is applied at all layers (Table 34, App. D). There is no position sweep, unlike Arditi et al.
statements.problem: Heretic on Gemma-2-2B is .847, not .84. The attack-site description leaves out that the direction comes from one token position and the edit is applied at all layers.

statements.correction: Llama-3.2-1B: matched attack INSEP .032±.008 vs base .540 (Table 10); disjoint CatQA corpus INSEP .033 vs base .489 (G.3); leaderboard INSEP .084 vs base .452 (Table 20). Mistral-7B-v0.3: INSEP .318 vs .720 (Table 23). Other INSEP bases ≤.097.
statements.problem: Pairs the matched-attack INSEP value (.032) with the disjoint-corpus undefended value (.489). These are two different conditions.

statements.correction: Undefended plain DIM edit (abl): Phi-4 .097, Gemma-2-2B .121, OLMo-2-1B .320, Llama-3.2-1B .452 (.540 in Table 10), OLMo-2-13B .484, Qwen3-14B .647, Mistral .720, Qwen2.5-7B .801. Heretic: .563 (OLMo-2-13B) to .928 (Qwen3-14B), above abl on all eight.
statements.problem: The .32–.54 range covers only Llama-3.2-1B, OLMo-2-1B and OLMo-2-13B. Across all eight undefended bases the plain edit spans .097–.801. Heretic is higher on every base.

statements.correction: Table 11 means over eight bases (Llama-3.2-1B to Qwen3-14B): ReFAT abl .643 vs .455, prefill .503 vs .339. Per base, ReFAT abl is higher than undefended on 5 (e.g. Phi-4 .819 vs .097) and lower on Mistral .588 vs .720, Qwen2.5 .734 vs .801, Qwen3 .582 vs .647. ReFAT is reimplemented with no public code.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the stated scope '7–14B instruct models' is wrong for this study: the means cover eight bases from 1B to 14B. Per base, ReFAT lowers ablation harm on three models.

statements.correction: ReFAT is reimplemented from its paper and retrained on all eight bases. .643 is their mean. Llama-3.2-1B: ReFAT abl .637 vs base .452 (Table 20). No Llama-3-8B is tested. The outcome is StrongREJECT harm.
statements.problem: The text does state ReFAT's models: it is retrained on each of the eight bases. None of them is Llama-3-8B, the model this conflict is about.

statements.correction: Per base, undefended SOM exceeds DIM on 5 of 8 bases and is lower on 3 (Mistral, Qwen2.5, Qwen3), which fits 'not reliably'.

The bases are named in Section 4. SOM: 4x4 hexagonal map, sigma .33, lr .01, 10,000 iterations, sharing DIM's contrast estimate (Table 34, App. D).

INSEP minimizes harmful–benign separability along a recomputed DIM direction, using refusal, compliance and prefill NLL terms (Eq. 3). On Llama-3.2-1B the behavioural terms alone resist abl (abl harm .054 with the separability term off, Table 7).
